a: Malicious software: programs written to cause harm or gain access
Software that is out of date
tasks.fb: Malware is a broad term covering viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware and spyware.

tasks.q: Which is the most common way malware reaches a computer?
a: A user opens an infected email attachment or download
By the computer being too old
tasks.fb: Most malware still needs a person to open something.

a: It attaches to files, and spreads when those files are opened and shared
It travels through the network on its own
It disguises itself as useful software
It encrypts files and demands payment
tasks.fb: Needing a user to run it is what separates a virus from a worm.

tasks.q: Which of these could carry a virus?
a: A program file attached to an email
A blank USB stick that has been formatted
tasks.fb: Any file that can be run, or that contains macros, can carry a virus.

tasks.q: What makes a worm different from a virus?
a: A worm copies itself across a network without any user action
A worm needs a user to open a file
tasks.fb: That's why worms can spread through a whole network in minutes.

tasks.q: Which defence helps most against worms?
a: Keeping software and operating systems patched and up to date
tasks.fb: Worms exploit known weaknesses, which patches fix.

a: Malware disguised as legitimate software that the user installs themselves
Malware that copies itself across networks
Software that encrypts a hard drive by accident
tasks.fb: The disguise is the whole point: the user lets it in.

tasks.q: What does a backdoor let an attacker do?
a: Access the computer again later, without the normal login
tasks.fb: Backdoors let attackers return whenever they like.

a: Encrypts files and demands payment for the key to unlock them
tasks.fb: CryptoLocker, from lesson 1, is an example.

a: Spyware that records every key pressed, including passwords
tasks.fb: Keyloggers can be software or a small device plugged in behind the keyboard.

tasks.q: Which of these help protect against malware? Select all that apply.
opts: Anti-malware software kept up to date
correct: Anti-malware software kept up to date
tasks.fb: Backups don't stop an infection, but they mean you don't have to pay a ransom.

tasks.q: Which type of malware does each description match?
items: Attaches to a file and spreads when that file is shared
Copies itself across a network with no user action
Pretends to be a free game, then opens a backdoor
Encrypts every document and demands Bitcoin
Needs the user to run an infected program
Exploits a weakness in unpatched software to spread by itself
Downloaded as a 'video player update' that steals passwords
Displays a countdown and a payment demand
tasks.fb: The key differences: viruses need a user, worms don't, trojans disguise themselves, and ransomware wants money.

info.title: The first worm
info.text: The Morris worm of 1988 was one of the first. It was meant as an experiment, but it slowed thousands of computers and led to the first conviction under a US computer crime law.

info.title: WannaCry
info.text: In 2017, the WannaCry ransomware worm spread worldwide in hours and hit NHS hospitals, cancelling thousands of appointments. A patch already existed, but many systems hadn't installed it.

info.title: Signatures and behaviour
info.text: Anti-malware spots known malware by its 'signature', and unknown malware by watching for suspicious behaviour, such as a program encrypting lots of files.

info.title: Sandbox
info.text: Security researchers run suspected malware inside a sandbox: an isolated virtual machine where it can do no harm.

info.title: Not just PCs
info.text: Phones, smart TVs and even fridges can be infected. Any device that runs software can run malicious software.

info.title: 3-2-1 backups
info.text: A common rule is 3 copies of your data, on 2 types of storage, with 1 kept off-site. Ransomware can't encrypt a backup that isn't connected.
